title: Market-based environmental policy
log: 2026-11-01T14:46:37Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: The closest bank point, eco-environmental-policies-australia, covers four kinds of environmental policy (regulation, emissions limits, renewables support and market-based tools) rather than the market-based idea alone, and it does not frame the policy as an aggregate supply policy or as a cost now that protects resources for later generations, so a new point is safer than a loose match.

draft.title: Market-based environmental policy
card: Pollution is often a cost that firms do not pay. Market-based policies put a price on it, so firms must count it in their costs.
the government sets a limit on total emissions and issues permits. Firms that emit more must buy permits, and those that cut emissions can sell spare ones.
a charge on each tonne of greenhouse gas a firm emits. It raises the cost of polluting, so firms have a reason to cut emissions.
These policies change costs now, such as higher production costs for heavy polluters. The aim is to protect resources and the environment for future generations.
draft.remember: Pricing pollution raises costs today to protect the environment for later generations.

a.q: A government limits total emissions and lets firms trade permits. Which effect on a coal-fired power company is most likely?
opts: Its costs rise unless it cuts its emissions
Its costs fall because it receives free output
Its output is fixed by the government each year
Its costs stay the same whatever it emits
a.why: Under a permit system, emitting more means buying permits, so costs rise unless the firm cuts emissions. The fixed output option is wrong because firms choose how to respond to the price.
a.clue: What must a firm do to emit more?

b.q: A cement maker in Ballarat faces a new price on each tonne of emissions. Why do economists say the policy shifts costs from the future to now?
opts: Firms pay today to protect resources for later generations
Firms avoid all costs now and pay them in the future
Consumers gain a benefit now and nothing in the future
The government bans emissions so costs stop for good
b.why: The price raises the firm's costs today. The benefit is a healthier environment and more resources for later generations. The ban option is wrong because the policy prices emissions rather than banning them.
b.clue: Who pays first, and who benefits later?

a.best: Its costs rise unless it cuts its emissions

b.best: Firms pay today to protect resources for later generations
